scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The formal word 'striptease' was first documented in 1932, though public erotic disrobing dates back centuries.
Antiquity recorded instances such as ancient Greek auletrides, Roman Floralia festival dances, and the performances of 6th-century Byzantine Empress Theodora.
Early theatrical references emerged during the English Restoration in Aphra Behn's 1677 comedy The Rover and Thomas Otway's 1681 play The Soldier's Fortune.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Striptease functions primarily as erotic entertainment, social spectacle, and adult nightlife, though it also appears as sexual play between partners and in private celebrations such as bachelor and bachelorette parties.
In 1957, semiotician Roland Barthes analyzed Parisian striptease in Mythologies as a reassuring ritual that dramatizes and exorcises erotic tension through glitz and theatrical distance.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: The performance typically follows a classic burlesque structure: entering fully costumed, baring the upper body first, and progressing toward the lower body and pelvic reveal.
Movement is built around sensual pacing, hip isolations, shimmies, and the rhythmic removal of individual garments.
Performers prolong the tease by holding removed clothing or hands in front of freshly exposed areas, or wearing nested layers.
Watch for The Bump and Grind, The Shimmy, The Fan Concealment.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Music provides the atmospheric frame and tempo for the dancer's physical expression.
In early vaudeville, burlesque, and British music halls, live pit bands played dramatic orchestrations, blues brass, and jazz beats tailored to the bump 'n grind.
Listen for the Tenor saxophone, Muted trumpet, Drum kit, Bass guitar.
The pulse is 4/4 at about 80 beats a minute.
A slow, low-register brass and saxophone groove accompanied by steady snare backbeats and walking basslines, creating a tension-and-release cadence that mirrors the performer's deliberate undressing.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Costuming is fundamental to striptease because the dance cannot exist without clothes to discard.

Traditional costumes incorporate glitzy sequins, feathers, layered petticoats, gloves, stockings, and ornate corsetry, often referencing character archetypes like brides, nurses, or vintage showgirls.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Iconic figures include Dutch dancer Mata Hari, who debuted her progressive disrobing act at the Musée Guimet in 1905; American burlesque legends Gypsy Rose Lee, Sally Rand, and Georgia Sothern; French revue stars Germaine Aymos and Josephine Baker; British theatre producer Phyllis Dixey; San Francisco pioneer Carol Doda; modern burlesque revivalist Dita Von Teese; and male revue companies like the Chippendales.

In Britain, 1930s censorship forced London's Windmill Theatre to invent motionless tableaux vivants and fan dances, which evolved by the 1970s into pub striptease across London's East End where dancers collected fees in beer jugs.

Tracing lines through theatrical pantomime, Ottoman-era Ghawazee dances documented by French travelers, and 19th-century hoochie-coochie fairground shows, striptease evolved into early 20th-century American burlesque and Parisian cabaret effeuillage.

scenes.title: Family tree
narration: Striptease is parent of Burlesque: Classic American burlesque comedy and variety shows provided the primary stage circuit where striptease routines developed.
Striptease is child of Pole dance: Developed inside late 20th-century exotic dance clubs before expanding into an athletic and acrobatic discipline worldwide.
Striptease is variant of Lap dance: A modern personalized strip club variant popularized at venues like San Francisco's Mitchell Brothers O'Farrell Theatre in 1980.
Striptease is influence of Go-go dancing: Topless 1960s go-go dancing merged with burlesque traditions to birth modern commercial club striptease.

visual_brief.costume_notes: Costuming is fundamental to striptease because the dance cannot exist without clothes to discard. Traditional costumes incorporate glitzy sequins, feathers, layered petticoats, gloves, stockings, and ornate corsetry, often referencing character archetypes like brides, nurses, or vintage showgirls. Settings range historically from opulent Parisian music halls and London Windmill Theatre tableaux to East End British pubs, Soho private clubs, and modern purpose-built strip clubs equipped with stages, vertical poles, and private lap-dancing booths.
visual_brief.setting_notes: Striptease functions primarily as erotic entertainment, social spectacle, and adult nightlife, though it also appears as sexual play between partners and in private celebrations such as bachelor and bachelorette parties. In 1957, semiotician Roland Barthes analyzed Parisian striptease in Mythologies as a reassuring ritual that dramatizes and exorcises erotic tension through glitz and theatrical distance. The late 20th-century New Burlesque revival repositioned striptease as an empowering, satirical performance art challenging narrow commercial beauty standards, recognized in December 2006 by a Norwegian court as a tax-exempt art form.
